# Analysis {#sec-analysis}

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

engine=create_engine(os.environ["AUTORACK_URL"])
df=pd.read_sql("""
select ca.county_fips, ca.year, ca.affordability_salary,
    cte.routine_cognitive_share, cte.routine_manual_share,
    cte.non_routine_cognitive_share, cte.non_routine_manual_share,
    cb.poverty_rate, cb.unemployment_rate, cb.population
from county_affordability ca
join county_task_exposure cte on ca.county_fips=cte.county_fips and ca.year=cte.year
join county_baseline cb on ca.county_fips=cb.county_fips and ca.year=cb.year
""", engine)
df["log_population"]=np.log(df["population"])
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# level model: OLS with year indicators, standard errors clustered by county
reg_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share",
          "poverty_rate","unemployment_rate","log_population"]

reg=df.dropna(subset=reg_cols+["affordability_salary"]).copy()

X=pd.concat([reg[reg_cols],
             pd.get_dummies(reg["year"], prefix="year", drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
X=sm.add_constant(X)

model=sm.OLS(reg["affordability_salary"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})

reg["fitted"]=model.fittedvalues
reg["resid"]=model.resid

# log respecification, same design matrix
reg["actual_log"]=np.log(reg["affordability_salary"])
model_log=sm.OLS(reg["actual_log"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})
reg["resid_log"]=model_log.resid
```

## Panel regression

The four task group values described in @eq-group sum to one, so all four cannot enter a
regression together. One serves as the reference category, and we use non routine
cognitive. Each remaining coefficient represents the change in affordability salary
associated with a shift out of non routine cognitive work and into that group, holding
the controls fixed. Each coefficient is a comparison against the reference category. The
group values are measured on a zero to one scale. Per percentage point figures reported
later therefore divide the estimated coefficients by 100.

Normalizing the four totals by their sum, as @sec-data describes, also resolves a
collinearity issue. Left unresolved, that issue would render these coefficients unusable.
The unnormalized totals in @eq-weighted exhibit variance inflation factors ranging from
13 to 27. All four are employment counts, so they scale together with county size.
Dividing by the four group sum removes this common scale and reduces the variance
inflation factors to approximately 1.

Year indicators capture conditions common to all counties within a year. These include
the 2008 recession, the recovery through the 2010s, and the price movement that
affordability salary does not itself account for. Standard errors are clustered by
county, because repeated observations of the same county across fifteen years are not
independent draws.

## Validation before modeling

Before making any estimations, we ensure that the data support the chosen methods. We examine the distributions of the four task groups and the affordability salary to identify any skewness or outliers. Additionally, we verify that the county-year coverage is consistent across the retained panel. Furthermore, we check for any overlap between task groups to ensure that no two groups effectively carry the same information. Figure @fig-dists provides visual representations of the distributions.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dists
#| fig-cap: "Distributions across the 12,087 county year panel. Affordability salary is right skewed with a long upper tail; the four task groups each show real cross county spread, with non routine cognitive the largest category."

share_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share",
            "non_routine_cognitive_share","non_routine_manual_share"]

titles=["Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual","Non Routine Cognitive","Non Routine Manual"]

layout=[["afford","afford"],
        ["rc","rm"],
        ["nrc","nrm"]]

fig, axes=plt.subplot_mosaic(layout, figsize=(6.5, 3))

sns.histplot(data=df, x="affordability_salary", bins=50, ax=axes["afford"])
axes["afford"].set_title("Affordability Salary ($)")
axes["afford"].set_xlabel("")

for key, col, title in zip(["rc","rm","nrc","nrm"], share_cols, titles):
    sns.histplot(data=df, x=col, bins=50, color="#009E73", ax=axes[key])
    axes[key].set_title(title)
    axes[key].set_xlabel("")
    axes[key].set_ylabel("")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Affordability salaries are right-skewed, with a skewness of 1.17. The center of the distribution is located near \$57,000, and a long tail of high-paying counties extends above it. This skewness is why the diagnostics below focus on the extremes of the distribution.

## Specification diagnostics

A linear model assumes a constant rate of association across the data range and symmetrical, evenly distributed errors around the fit. We verify these assumptions using three diagnostics: residuals plotted against fitted values, a QQ plot of the residuals, and variance inflation factors. @fig-resid-analysis illustrates the first two diagnostics, pinpointing the failure directly. The smoothed residual line deviates from zero, indicating a non-linear relationship. The vertical spread of residuals increases with fitted values. The model underestimates both the least and most affordable counties while fitting the middle well. Additionally, the QQ plot deviates from normality in the upper tail, suggesting a residual skew of 1.02.

```{python}
#| label: fig-resid-analysis
#| fig-cap: "Level model diagnostics. Left: residuals against fitted values with lowess smoother; the curve away from zero at both ends shows the model underpredicting the least and most affordable counties. Right: QQ plot of residuals; the bend above the line in the upper tail reflects the residual skew of 1.02."

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,4))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#D55E00"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Affordability Salary ($)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual ($)")

stats.probplot(reg["resid"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The level model still provides the interpretable estimates we report. Additionally, its own diagnostics demonstrate that the data possess a structure that a straight line in dollars cannot adequately represent. Binned means plots in @sec-results illustrate the underprediction in dollar terms, with approximately \$8,000 to \$9,000 of underprediction at each tail.

## Log respecification

Underprediction at both extremes is a hallmark of a multiplicative process that is fitted on an additive scale. The factors influencing affordability operate proportionally, resulting in a more significant impact on a high-affordability county compared to a low-affordability one when a similar change occurs in an input variable. By converting the proportional effects into the additive form assumed by linear models, we refit the same specification on log affordability salary. Consequently, the diagnostics respond accordingly, as demonstrated by @fig-log-diag. The residual skew decreases from 1.02 to 0.09, and the spread becomes relatively constant across the fitted range. The QQ plot also straightens through most of its range. The log linear fit serves as the baseline for evaluating the flexible models presented in the subsequent section.

```{python}
#| label: fig-log-diag
#| fig-cap: "Log model diagnostics, same layout as the level model. The smoother lies close to zero, the spread is near constant, and the QQ plot tracks the diagonal through most of its range, showing the transformation resolves most of the level model's failure."


reg["fitted_log"]=model_log.fittedvalues

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,4))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#009E73"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Log Affordability Salary")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual")

stats.probplot(reg["resid_log"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The smoothed residual line doesn’t lie perfectly flat even after the transformation. The remaining deviations are structured in a way that a single global transformation cannot absorb, most likely due to interactions among the inputs. These deviations motivate the increase in model complexity.

## Variance decomposition

Affordability, salary, and task groups vary both across counties and within a county over time. These variations have different implications. The two manual groups show almost complete variation between counties, with only 10-25% variation within a county on the corrected window. This makes the associated affordability differences more durable rather than temporary. Routine cognitive is the only group with genuine within-county movement, with nearly half of its variation on the corrected window.

The Census occupation coding change between 2009 and 2010, as described in @sec-data, inflates apparent within-county variation for the routine cognitive group. This is due to the way the source data were coded, not a property of the counties. Therefore, we repeat the main estimates on a panel restricted to 2010 onward and additionally on pre-pandemic (2010-2019) and post-pandemic (2021-2023) windows. Coefficient stability across these windows is reported in @sec-results, along with the between- versus within-county exhibits that support the claim of persistence.

## Predictive Modeling

Beyond the inferential panel regression above, we evaluate three predictive
approaches of increasing complexity: linear regression, Random Forest, and a
small neural net. We check whether a flexible model captures meaningfully more
signal than the linear specification. We reuse the county-year panel already
assembled above, extended with state identifiers for the fixed effects
comparison below.

```{python}
#| include: false
# state_code isn't in the panel regression's df, add it here
state_lookup = pd.read_sql(
    "select county_fips, state_code from county", engine
)
df_ml = df.merge(state_lookup, on="county_fips", how="left")
```

### Feature set and reference categories

```{python}
#| include: false
feature_cols = [
    "routine_cognitive_share",
    "routine_manual_share",
    "non_routine_cognitive_share",
    "non_routine_manual_share",
    "poverty_rate",
    "unemployment_rate",
    "year",
    "state_code",
]

model_df = df_ml.dropna(subset=feature_cols).copy()
model_df[feature_cols].describe(include="all").T
```

Task shares are computed directly by the database as each category's count
divided by the four-category sum, so they already satisfy the constraint used
in the panel regression above and require no additional normalization here.
As before, one category must be dropped to avoid a deterministic column, and
we retain `non_routine_cognitive_share` as the omitted reference for
consistency with the panel regression.

### Year and state dummies

Running year as a factor, not as numeric, gives each year its own independent
coefficient, with no assumption about ordering or spacing between them.

Leaving one state as a reference state as well, which will be the median
affordability state, whatever that may be in our data.

```{python}
model_df["year"] = model_df["year"].astype("category")
model_df["state_code"] = model_df["state_code"].astype("category")

REFERENCE_YEAR = model_df["year"].cat.categories.min()      # earliest year as reference

# Pool states with too few counties to support a stable, independent coefficient
county_counts = model_df.groupby("state_code", observed=True)["county_fips"].nunique()
THIN_STATE_THRESHOLD = 5
thin_states = county_counts[county_counts < THIN_STATE_THRESHOLD].index.tolist()
print("States pooled into 'OTHER' (fewer than", THIN_STATE_THRESHOLD, "counties):", thin_states)

model_df["state_code_grouped"] = model_df["state_code"].astype(str)
model_df["state_code_grouped"] = model_df["state_code_grouped"].where(
    ~model_df["state_code_grouped"].isin(thin_states), "OTHER"
)
model_df["state_code_grouped"] = model_df["state_code_grouped"].astype("category")

state_affordability = model_df.groupby("state_code_grouped", observed=True)["affordability_salary"].mean().sort_values()
print(state_affordability)

median_state = state_affordability.index[len(state_affordability) // 2]
print("\nState/group closest to median affordability:", median_state)

REFERENCE_STATE = median_state

year_dummies = pd.get_dummies(model_df["year"], prefix="year")
year_dummies = year_dummies.drop(columns=[f"year_{REFERENCE_YEAR}"])

state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(model_df["state_code_grouped"], prefix="state")
state_dummies = state_dummies.drop(columns=[f"state_{REFERENCE_STATE}"])

model_df = pd.concat([model_df, year_dummies, state_dummies], axis=1)

year_cols_model = list(year_dummies.columns)
state_cols_model = list(state_dummies.columns)

print("Year dummy columns:", year_cols_model)
print("Number of state dummy columns:", len(state_cols_model))
```

Here we identify every state with fewer than 5 distinct counties in our data
and relabel them as "OTHER." They can't reliably support their own
independent coefficient otherwise.

Texas was selected as the reference state because its mean affordability sits
closest to the panel median. It's not a cost-of-living outlier in either
direction, and it has enormous within-state diversity: major metros like
Austin/Dallas/Houston alongside a huge number of rural counties. So,
"different from Texas" is a fairly intuitive baseline for other states to be
read against.

```{python}
#| label: fig-state-afford
#| fig-cap: "Mean affordability salary by state, sorted ascending, with the panel median marked. Texas sits near the middle of the distribution, supporting its use as the reference state."

state_affordability.plot(kind="bar", figsize=(14, 4))
plt.axhline(state_affordability.median(), color="red", linestyle="--", label="Median")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

Figure @fig-state-afford shows that Texas lies near the middle of the states
in terms of affordability and is usable as a reference point.

### Collinearity check

Our four main features — `routine_cognitive_share`, `routine_manual_share`,
`non_routine_cognitive_share`, `non_routine_manual_share` — are shares of a
whole, thus we need to remove one in order to maintain independence (as the
fourth is deterministic once you know the values of the other three). If we
didn't remove one, then one feature for certain would be a VIF offender.

The remaining three coefficients become interpretable as: the effect of
shifting share toward this category, away from the omitted one.

```{python}
exposure_check_cols = ["routine_cognitive_share",
    "routine_manual_share",
    "non_routine_cognitive_share",
    "non_routine_manual_share"]

REFERENCE_EXPOSURE = "non_routine_cognitive_share"
exposure_cols_model = [c for c in exposure_check_cols if c != REFERENCE_EXPOSURE]
core_features = exposure_cols_model + ["poverty_rate", "unemployment_rate"]
print("Exposure scores entering the model:", exposure_cols_model)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-vif-ml
#| tbl-cap: "Variance inflation factors for year and state dummies after removing the reference exposure category. All values fall below 5, indicating no remaining collinearity concern."
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
import statsmodels.api as sm

vif_features = core_features + year_cols_model + state_cols_model

X_vif = sm.add_constant(model_df[vif_features].astype(float))

vif_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": X_vif.columns,
    "VIF": [variance_inflation_factor(X_vif.values, i) for i in range(X_vif.shape[1])],
})
vif_data[vif_data["feature"].isin(year_cols_model + state_cols_model)].sort_values("VIF", ascending=False).head(10)
```

@tbl-vif-ml lists the highest variance inflation factors after removal of
`non_routine_cognitive_share`; no offender columns remain, as all features
have VIF < 5.

### Train/test split (grouped by county)

Not forecasting, so a time-ordered split isn't required for its usual reason.
But we do want a grouped split because a county's economic profile likely
barely moves year to year, so its 2018 and 2019 rows are near-duplicates.
Obviously, this is a problem, as if two sequential rows end up in opposite
splits, the model can just memorize rather than learn relationships. So, we
will group by `county_fips` when splitting to force every test-set prediction
to come from a county the model has never seen a single row of. This ensures
a test of whether the pattern is relationship driven rather than memorized.

```{python}
#| include: false
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

feature_cols_reg = core_features + year_cols_model + state_cols_model
target_col = "affordability_salary"


X = model_df[feature_cols_reg].reset_index(drop=True).astype(float)
y = model_df[target_col].reset_index(drop=True)
groups = model_df["county_fips"].reset_index(drop=True)

# quick skew check on the target -- log-transform candidate
print("Target skew:", y.skew())

gss = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
train_idx, test_idx = next(gss.split(X, y, groups))

X_train, X_test = X.iloc[train_idx], X.iloc[test_idx]
y_train, y_test = y.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[test_idx]
groups_train = groups.iloc[train_idx]

print("Train rows:", len(X_train), " Test rows:", len(X_test))
print("Overlap in county_fips between train/test (should be 0):",
      len(set(groups.iloc[train_idx]) & set(groups.iloc[test_idx])))
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# Baseline feature set (no year/state), reusing the SAME row split as the full model
feature_cols_base = exposure_cols_model + ["poverty_rate", "unemployment_rate"]
X_base = model_df[feature_cols_base].reset_index(drop=True).astype(float)
X_train_base, X_test_base = X_base.iloc[train_idx], X_base.iloc[test_idx]
```

### Linear regression: baseline vs. full model

We report two versions of each linear model throughout this section: a
**baseline** (exposure shares + poverty + unemployment only) and a **full**
model (baseline + year and state controls). The baseline establishes what the
relationship looks like without accounting for time/geography; the full model
is what we carry forward as our primary result, as it's the more rigorous
version. Including both lets us demonstrate exactly what changes when
time/geography are accounted for, and why.

#### Baseline OLS (no year/state)

```{python}
X_train_base_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train_base)
ols_model_base = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_base_sm).fit()
print(ols_model_base.summary())
```

(Note that features are on wildly different scales.) R² = 0.766 is
respectable. Every coefficient is negative and highly significant, which
makes sense given that non-routine cognitive was our reference, and shifting
county task mix toward any of the other categories is associated with lower
affordability (though non-routine manual is the steepest).

NOTE: If we were doing predictions, the target skewness might be an issue and
a log transform would be worth considering — tabled for now since we're not
forecasting.

#### Full OLS (with year/state controls)

```{python}
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train)
ols_model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()
print(ols_model.params[core_features])
print("R-squared:", ols_model.rsquared)
```

With the addition of time and geography, the R² increased from 0.766 to 0.871
in the same model, implying that these variables explain real variance.
Notably, the `unemployment_rate` coefficient flips sign, meaning that the
baseline coefficient likely absorbed some of the geography and time
confounding. This makes sense as unemployment-heavy places/times also tend to
be low-affordability places/times. The full model's coefficient reflects the
within-state-year relationship instead. Also notable, the exposure mix
coefficients maintained their direction and relative ordering through the
addition of the new features.

Figure @fig-ols-diag shows both diagnostics side by side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ols-diag
#| fig-cap: "Full raw-target OLS diagnostics. Left: residuals against fitted values; the U-shaped pattern shows the model underpredicting at both extremes. Right: QQ plot of residuals, deviating from normality in the upper tail."

import scipy.stats as stats

fitted_ols = ols_model.predict(X_train_sm)
residuals_ols = y_train - fitted_ols

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))

axes[0].scatter(fitted_ols, residuals_ols, alpha=0.3, s=10)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted values")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residuals")
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")

stats.probplot(residuals_ols, dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

There is a clear U-shaped pattern to the residual plot, indicating that the
residuals are not uniformly distributed, thus the OLS is not a reliable model
for our data with the target as is.

#### Full OLS (with year/state controls) and log target

The binned affordability salary vs. affordability salary graphs showed an
approximate exponential pattern, so we will investigate whether logging the
target will make a linear model more appropriate.

```{python}
print("Any zero/negative affordability values?", (y <= 0).sum())  # confirm log is safe

y_train_log = np.log(y_train)
y_test_log = np.log(y_test)

print("Skew, original:", y_train.skew())
print("Skew, logged:  ", y_train_log.skew())

ols_model_log = sm.OLS(y_train_log, X_train_sm).fit()
print(ols_model_log.summary())
```

Figure @fig-ols-log-diag shows the same pair of diagnostics for the
log-target specification.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ols-log-diag
#| fig-cap: "Log-target OLS diagnostics, same layout as the raw-target model. The residual spread is roughly constant across fitted values and the QQ plot tracks the diagonal much more closely."

residuals_log = y_train_log - ols_model_log.predict(X_train_sm)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))

axes[0].scatter(ols_model_log.predict(X_train_sm), residuals_log, alpha=0.3, s=10)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted (log)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residuals (log)")
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")

stats.probplot(residuals_log, dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The residual plot looks uniformly distributed and the QQ plot follows a
straight line pattern, so with a logged target we can use a linear model.

```{python}
print("R-squared (log target, in-sample):", ols_model_log.rsquared)

X_test_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test, has_constant="add")
y_pred_ols_log = ols_model_log.predict(X_test_sm)

print("Test R2 (log space):", r2_score(y_test_log, y_pred_ols_log))

y_pred_ols_log_dollars = np.exp(y_pred_ols_log)
print("Test R2 (back-transformed to $):", r2_score(y_test, y_pred_ols_log_dollars))
print("Test MAE (back-transformed to $):", mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_ols_log_dollars))
```

With a logged target, the model achieves an in-sample R² of 0.913 and a
held-out test R² (transformed back into dollars) of 0.896. Both are notably
higher than the raw-target model's 0.871, and with valid residual
diagnostics.

#### Baseline vs. full comparison table

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ols-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Coefficients across the baseline, full raw-target, and full log-target OLS specifications, with log-target coefficients also converted to percent change per one-point shift."

comparison_ols = pd.DataFrame({
    "baseline": ols_model_base.params,
    "with_controls (raw $)": ols_model.params[feature_cols_base],
    "with_controls (log target)": ols_model_log.params[feature_cols_base],
})

log_coefs = ols_model_log.params[feature_cols_base]

# exposure shares are 0-1 scale (1pp = 0.01 units); poverty/unemployment are already in point units (1pp = 1 unit)
unit_per_point = {
    "routine_cognitive_share": 0.01,
    "routine_manual_share": 0.01,
    "non_routine_manual_share": 0.01,
    "poverty_rate": 1.0,
    "unemployment_rate": 1.0,
}

pct_change_per_point = {
    feat: (np.exp(log_coefs[feat] * unit_per_point[feat]) - 1) * 100
    for feat in feature_cols_base
}

comparison_ols["log_target (% change per 1pp)"] = pd.Series(pct_change_per_point)
comparison_ols
```

As @tbl-ols-comparison shows, `unemployment_rate`'s sign flip is confirmed
across all three fitted forms. Exposure coefficients shrink in magnitude from
baseline to raw-controls while `poverty_rate` grows (−1,376.50 → −1,728.82).

Each additional percentage point of poverty rate is associated with roughly a
2.9% decrease in affordability, holding time, geography, and task-mix fixed.
This is a considerably larger proportional effect than any single task-mix
category.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ols-r2-summary
#| tbl-cap: "R-squared by specification stage: baseline, full raw-target (diagnostics failed), and full log-target."

r2_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["Baseline OLS", "Full OLS (raw $, diagnostics failed)", "Full OLS (log target)"],
    "r2_or_note": [ols_model_base.rsquared, ols_model.rsquared, ols_model_log.rsquared],
})
r2_summary
```

@tbl-ols-r2-summary shows R² climbing through each stage of this analysis. First, adding year and state
controls to the baseline model (0.766 → 0.871) confirms that time and
geography explain real, previously unmodeled variance. Logging the target
(0.871 → 0.913 in-sample, 0.896 held-out) accounts for even more variance once
the residual violations from the raw-target model are resolved. This is the
model used for inference going forward, since the raw-target model's
coefficient significance cannot be trusted given its failed residual
diagnostics above.

### Random Forest

For a Random Forest (RF), we performed a grid search using `n_estimators`,
`max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, and `max_features` over the grid shown
below. Given a high number of estimators to reduce variance, and
`max_depth`/`min_samples_leaf` to add potential regularization.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Grid search actually run once; shown here for documentation of the search
# space. Not re-executed on every render — see the following chunk for the
# cached result.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, GroupKFold

rf = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": [600, 1000],
    "max_depth": [None, 10, 20],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5],
    "max_features": [1.0, "sqrt", 0.5],
}

group_cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
gcv = GridSearchCV(rf, param_grid, cv=group_cv, scoring="r2", n_jobs=-1)
gcv.fit(X_train, y_train, groups=groups_train)

print("Best params:", gcv.best_params_)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# Grid search above was run once over the full param_grid; best params found were: 
# {'max_depth': None, 'max_features': 0.5, 'min_samples_leaf': 1, 'n_estimators': 1000}
# Hardcoded here to avoid re-running an expensive search on every render.
best_params = {
    "max_depth": None,
    "max_features": 0.5,
    "min_samples_leaf": 1,
    "n_estimators": 1000,
}

best_rf = RandomForestRegressor(**best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=2)
best_rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_rf = best_rf.predict(X_test)
print("Test R2: ", r2_score(y_test, y_pred_rf))
print("Test MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_rf))

# overfitting check
print("Train R2:", best_rf.score(X_train, y_train))
```

An R² of 0.876 is higher than the raw-target OLS model (0.871), suggesting at
least some non-linear relationship in the data at this stage. However, as
shown above, this comparison changes once the target is log-transformed,
which will be addressed in the comparison below.

A train/test gap of 0.989 vs. 0.876 tells us that the ceiling on this feature
set is being constrained by something other than hyperparameters. We are
already fitting training data about as well as a tree ensemble can, we just
aren't getting better generalization.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rf-resid
#| fig-cap: "Random Forest residuals against predicted values on the held-out test set. No systematic curve or trend is visible across the range of predictions."

residuals_rf = y_test - y_pred_rf

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.scatter(y_pred_rf, residuals_rf, alpha=0.3, s=10, color="green")
plt.axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("Predicted values")
plt.ylabel("Residuals")
plt.title("Random Forest residuals vs. predicted (test)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Unlike the raw-target OLS residuals, Figure @fig-rf-resid shows Random
Forest's residuals with no systematic curve or trend across the range of
predicted values.

```{python}
#| include: false

```

##### Ablation test

```{python}
feature_cols_no_exposure = [c for c in feature_cols_reg if c not in exposure_cols_model]
X_train_ne = X_train[feature_cols_no_exposure]
X_test_ne = X_test[feature_cols_no_exposure]

rf_no_exposure = RandomForestRegressor(**best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
rf_no_exposure.fit(X_train_ne, y_train)
print("R2 without exposure scores:", rf_no_exposure.score(X_test_ne, y_test))
```

Without accounting for automatability at all, the same Random Forest achieves
an R² of 0.834.

##### Reverse ablation test

```{python}
feature_cols_no_econ = [c for c in feature_cols_reg if c not in ["poverty_rate", "unemployment_rate"]]
X_train_ne2 = X_train[feature_cols_no_econ]
X_test_ne2 = X_test[feature_cols_no_econ]

rf_no_econ = RandomForestRegressor(**best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
rf_no_econ.fit(X_train_ne2, y_train)
print("R2 without poverty/unemployment:", rf_no_econ.score(X_test_ne2, y_test))
```

Using only the automatability scores (excluding poverty and unemployment),
the model reaches an R² of 0.698 — meaningful on its own, but well short of
the full model.

##### Testing RF with logged target

Logging the target could be good for RF too, so we run that as well.

```{python}
rf_log = RandomForestRegressor(**best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=2)
rf_log.fit(X_train, y_train_log)

y_pred_rf_log = rf_log.predict(X_test)
print("Test R2 (log space):", r2_score(y_test_log, y_pred_rf_log))

y_pred_rf_log_dollars = np.exp(y_pred_rf_log)
print("Test R2 (back-transformed to $):", r2_score(y_test, y_pred_rf_log_dollars))
print("Test MAE (back-transformed to $):", mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_rf_log_dollars))
```

An R² of 0.877 after back-transforming — a negligible change from the
untransformed-target model (0.876). Since the log-target model is already
established as the reference model for the linear regression above, we adopt
log-target RF here as well for consistency in the final comparison, even
though the choice of target makes little practical difference for Random
Forest specifically.

#### Grouped permutation — the actual "combination" question

To see what the four exposure scores do together, rather than one at a time
diluting each other, we permute all four jointly and compare the drop in R²
to permuting them individually.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score as _r2

exposure_cols = exposure_cols_model  # the three non-reference exposure scores
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

baseline_r2 = _r2(y_test, best_rf.predict(X_test))

def grouped_permutation_drop(cols, n_repeats=20):
    drops = []
    for _ in range(n_repeats):
        X_perm = X_test.copy()
        shuffled_idx = rng.permutation(len(X_perm))
        X_perm[cols] = X_perm[cols].values[shuffled_idx]
        drops.append(baseline_r2 - _r2(y_test, best_rf.predict(X_perm)))
    return np.mean(drops)

print("Baseline R2:", baseline_r2)

joint_drop = grouped_permutation_drop(exposure_cols)
print("Drop from permuting all exposure scores together:", joint_drop)

individual_drops = {}
for col in exposure_cols:
    individual_drops[col] = grouped_permutation_drop([col])
    print(f"Drop from permuting {col} alone:", individual_drops[col])

year_drop = grouped_permutation_drop(year_cols_model)
state_drop = grouped_permutation_drop(state_cols_model)
print("Drop from permuting year (jointly):", year_drop)
print("Drop from permuting state (jointly):", state_drop)
```

Year matters far more than state (0.127 vs. 0.008): time, not geography,
carries the bulk of the "when/where" signal once economic and exposure score
variables are controlled for.

Exposure score gross importance (0.153) is considerably larger than its
net/irreplaceable contribution of 0.042 from the ablation test in RF. This
implies that it shares (mostly) real predictive overlap with poverty,
unemployment, and time, but still adds something those don't fully capture.

Among the three individual task shares, `non_routine_manual_share` shows the
largest individual sensitivity (though none of the three should be read as
independently additive given they are parts of a whole).

### Simple neural net

We will build a simple neural net. As it is likely already a bit overkill, we
will keep it shallow and the layers narrow. We are still doing a regression
and our target is continuous, so we will have a single linear output unit.

```{python}
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models, callbacks

scaler_x = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
X_train_s = scaler_x.transform(X_train)
X_test_s = scaler_x.transform(X_test)

scaler_y = StandardScaler().fit(y_train.values.reshape(-1, 1))
y_train_s = scaler_y.transform(y_train.values.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
y_test_s = scaler_y.transform(y_test.values.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()

n_features = X_train.shape[1]          # now ~70+ with year/state dummies
h1 = int(round(n_features * 1.5))
h2 = max(int(round(h1 * 0.5)), 20)
h3 = 10                                  # latent bottleneck

nn = models.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(n_features,)),
    layers.Dense(h1, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dropout(0.2),
    layers.Dense(h2, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dropout(0.2),
    layers.Dense(h3, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(1, activation="linear"),   # regression head
])

nn.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])

es = callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=15, restore_best_weights=True)

history = nn.fit(
    X_train_s, y_train_s,
    validation_split=0.2,
    epochs=300,
    batch_size=32,
    callbacks=[es],
    verbose=0,
)

y_pred_nn_s = nn.predict(X_test_s).ravel()
y_pred_nn = scaler_y.inverse_transform(y_pred_nn_s.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()

print("Test R2: ", r2_score(y_test, y_pred_nn))
print("Test MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_nn))
print("Stopped at epoch:", len(history.history["loss"]))
print("Best val_loss achieved:", min(history.history["val_loss"]))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-nn-curve-initial
#| fig-cap: "Training and validation loss for the initial, unregularized neural net. Training loss plateaus below 0.1 while validation loss falls to roughly 0.2 before rising to about 0.5, indicating overfitting."

plt.plot(history.history["loss"], label="train")
plt.plot(history.history["val_loss"], label="val")
plt.legend(); plt.title("NN training curve"); plt.show()
```

Figure @fig-nn-curve-initial shows training loss decreasing steadily and
plateauing below 0.1, while validation loss initially decreases to
approximately 0.2 before rising to roughly 0.5, a clear indication of
overfitting. We address this with L2 weight regularization, increased
dropout, and a shorter early-stopping patience.

```{python}
from tensorflow.keras import regularizers

nn = models.Sequential([
    layers.Input(shape=(n_features,)),
    layers.Dense(h1, activation="relu", kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(0.001)),
    layers.Dropout(0.4),
    layers.Dense(h2, activation="relu", kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(0.001)),
    layers.Dropout(0.3),
    layers.Dense(h3, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(1, activation="linear"),
])

nn.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])

es = callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=8, restore_best_weights=True)

history = nn.fit(
    X_train_s, y_train_s,
    validation_split=0.2,
    epochs=300,
    batch_size=32,
    callbacks=[es],
    verbose=0,
)

print("Stopped at epoch:", len(history.history["loss"]))
print("Best val_loss achieved:", min(history.history["val_loss"]))

y_pred_nn_s = nn.predict(X_test_s).ravel()
y_pred_nn = scaler_y.inverse_transform(y_pred_nn_s.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()

print("Test R2: ", r2_score(y_test, y_pred_nn))
print("Test MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_nn))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-nn-curve-regularized
#| fig-cap: "Training and validation loss after adding L2 regularization, increased dropout, and shorter early-stopping patience. The train/validation gap narrows relative to the initial model."

plt.plot(history.history["loss"], label="train")
plt.plot(history.history["val_loss"], label="val")
plt.legend(); plt.title("NN training curve"); plt.show()
```

Figure @fig-nn-curve-regularized shows the training curve after these
changes. Additional tuning could likely narrow the remaining gap between training and
validation loss further. However, the current results are sufficient to draw
the conclusion that the neural network does not outperform Random Forest or
the log-target linear model, both of which are substantially cheaper to fit
and tune. Given this project's emphasis on explaining the relationship
between job automatability and affordability rather than maximizing
predictive accuracy, we do not pursue further tuning of the neural network
and proceed with the linear and Random Forest models as our primary results.

### Cross validation

After exploring and comparing the explained variance of the three different
models, we cross-validate to give the models more generalizability.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cv-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and standard deviation of held-out R-squared across 5-fold grouped cross-validation for log-target OLS and Random Forest."

from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold

group_kfold_cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
cv_results = {"OLS (log target)": [], "Random Forest": []}

y_log = np.log(y)  # full-data log target, same idea as y_train_log/y_test_log

for fold, (tr_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(group_kfold_cv.split(X, y, groups)):
    X_tr, X_val = X.iloc[tr_idx], X.iloc[val_idx]
    y_tr, y_val = y.iloc[tr_idx], y.iloc[val_idx]
    y_tr_log, y_val_log = y_log.iloc[tr_idx], y_log.iloc[val_idx]

    X_tr_sm = sm.add_constant(X_tr)
    X_val_sm = sm.add_constant(X_val, has_constant="add")
    ols_fold_log = sm.OLS(y_tr_log, X_tr_sm).fit()
    pred_log = ols_fold_log.predict(X_val_sm)
    r2_ols_log_dollars = r2_score(y_val, np.exp(pred_log))  # back-transformed, dollar scale
    cv_results["OLS (log target)"].append(r2_ols_log_dollars)

    rf_fold = RandomForestRegressor(**best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
    rf_fold.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    r2_rf = r2_score(y_val, rf_fold.predict(X_val))
    cv_results["Random Forest"].append(r2_rf)

    print(f"Fold {fold}: OLS(log)={r2_ols_log_dollars:.3f} RF={r2_rf:.3f}")

cv_summary = pd.DataFrame({m: {"mean_r2": np.mean(s), "std_r2": np.std(s)} for m, s in cv_results.items()}).T
cv_summary
```

As @tbl-cv-summary shows, across 5-fold cross-validation, OLS (log target)
and Random Forest are statistically indistinguishable (mean R² of 0.901 and
0.901, respectively),
with Random Forest showing marginally lower variance across folds (std
0.0090 vs. 0.0095). This confirms the single-split result below is not an
artifact of one particular split, and both models generalize consistently
and comparably across held-out counties.

Note that the neural net was not included, as cross-validating would be very
expensive, and as noted above it will not be carried forward for that reason.

Model comparison across test R² and MAE, along with the full ablation-test
takeaways, appears in @sec-results.

## Wrap-up summary

Three specifications answer three different questions. The panel regression, with
county-clustered standard errors, is the model we use for inference. It tells us that
routine-intensive work is associated with lower affordability salary even after
controlling for poverty, unemployment, time, and geography. Its log respecification
resolves the residual violations that make the raw target version untrustworthy for
that purpose.

The predictive models answer the different question of how much of affordability salary
can be explained at all, and by what. Random Forest and the log-target linear model
perform comparably on held-out data, which tells us the relationship's curvature adds
little once poverty, unemployment, time, and geography are already in the model. The
neural net does not improve on either, and its added complexity is not justified by
this feature set.

Across both approaches, task-mix shares carry real, independent explanatory power, but
poverty rate remains the dominant single factor throughout. This ordering, not any one
model's fit statistic, is the finding this analysis is built to support, and it is what
@sec-results carries forward.
